messages.content:
Compute the largest positive integer \( n \) such that

\[
n \text{ divides } (\lfloor \sqrt{n} \rfloor)!^{n!} + 450.
\]

Put your final answer within \boxed{}.

message.content:
Let

\[
m=\lfloor \sqrt n\rfloor,\qquad F=n!.
\]

We need

\[
n\mid (m!)^{F}+450.
\]

Also note

\[
450=2\cdot 3^2\cdot 5^2,\qquad 451=11\cdot 41.
\]

We will use two basic observations.

---

### 1. Prime factors \(p\le m\)

Suppose \(p^a\parallel n\) and \(p\le m\). Since \(p\mid m!\),

\[
v_p\!\left((m!)^F\right)=F\,v_p(m!)\ge F=n!\ge a.
\]

Thus

\[
(m!)^F\equiv 0 \pmod{p^a}.
\]

Since \(n\mid (m!)^F+450\), we must have

\[
p^a\mid 450.
\]

So any prime \(p\le m\) dividing \(n\) can only be \(2,3,5\), with exponents at most those in \(450\):

\[
v_2(n)\le 1,\qquad v_3(n)\le 2,\qquad v_5(n)\le 2.
\]

---

### 2. Prime factors \(p>m\)

Suppose \(p^a\parallel n\) and \(p>m\). First, \(a=1\), because if \(a\ge2\), then

\[
n\ge p^2\ge (m+1)^2,
\]

contradicting \(n<(m+1)^2\).

Now \(p\nmid m!\), and since \(p\mid n\), we have \(p\le n\), so \(p-1\mid n!=F\). By Fermat’s little theorem,

\[
(m!)^F\equiv 1 \pmod p.
\]

Therefore, for \(p\mid (m!)^F+450\), we need

\[
1+450=451\equiv 0\pmod p.
\]

Thus

\[
p\mid 451=11\cdot 41.
\]

So any prime factor of \(n\) larger than \(m\) must be \(11\) or \(41\), and only to the first power.

---

Now we bound \(m\).

If \(m\ge 41\), then the primes \(11\) and \(41\) are not larger than \(m\). Hence no prime factor of \(n\) can be larger than \(m\), and every prime factor of \(n\) must come from \(2,3,5\) with bounded exponents. Therefore \(n\mid 450\). But

\[
n\ge m^2\ge 41^2=1681>450,
\]

a contradiction. So

\[
m\le 40.
\]

If \(m\le 10\), then \(n\le 120\), which will not be maximal once we exhibit a larger valid \(n\).

Now consider

\[
11\le m\le 40.
\]

Since \(11\le m\), the prime \(11\) cannot divide \(n\). The only possible prime factor larger than \(m\) is therefore \(41\), and it can appear at most once. Hence

\[
n=d\quad\text{or}\quad n=41d,
\]

where \(d\mid 450\).

If \(n=d\), then \(n\le 450\).

If \(n=41d\), then since \(m\le 40\),

\[
n<41^2=1681,
\]

so

\[
d\le \left\lfloor \frac{1680}{41}\right\rfloor=40.
\]

The largest divisor of \(450\) not exceeding \(40\) is \(30\). Therefore

\[
n\le 41\cdot 30=1230.
\]

So no admissible \(n\) can exceed \(1230\).

It remains to verify that \(n=1230\) works. We have

\[
\lfloor\sqrt{1230}\rfloor=35,
\]

and

\[
1230=2\cdot 3\cdot 5\cdot 41=30\cdot 41.
\]

Since \(35!\) is divisible by \(30\), and \(450\) is divisible by \(30\),

\[
(35!)^{1230!}+450\equiv 0\pmod{30}.
\]

Modulo \(41\), since \(41>35\) and \(1230!\) is a multiple of \(40\),

\[
(35!)^{1230!}\equiv 1\pmod{41}.
\]

Also \(450=451-1\equiv -1\pmod{41}\), so

\[
(35!)^{1230!}+450\equiv 1-1\equiv 0\pmod{41}.
\]

Because \(30\) and \(41\) are coprime, the expression is divisible by

\[
30\cdot 41=1230.
\]

Thus the largest possible \(n\) is

\[
\boxed{1230}.
\]
